reply.text:
**`git merge --squash`** combines a branch into your current branch as one new commit. You run it on the target branch (say, `main`):

```
git switch main
git merge --squash feature
git commit        # one commit containing all of feature's changes
```

- It rewrites nothing. `feature` keeps its original commits.
- The result has no merge parent and no link to `feature`'s commits, so Git doesn't know the feature was merged. A later `git merge feature` can produce conflicts or re-apply changes you already took.

**Interactive rebase squash** (`git rebase -i`) rewrites the commits on your own branch. You mark commits as `squash` or `fixup` to fold them together, and you can reword messages or split the work into several commits:

```
git switch feature
git rebase -i main    # mark commits as squash/fixup in the editor
```

- It creates new commits with new hashes, so `feature`'s history changes. If you've already pushed the branch, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`.
- It only cleans up your branch. Nothing reaches `main` until you integrate it, for example with `git switch main && git merge --ff-only feature`.

**In short:** `merge --squash` is a one-shot way to land a branch on another branch as a single commit, with no history link. Interactive rebase tidies the commits on the branch itself and keeps the branch's history, though rewritten, so you can merge it normally afterward.

A common pattern is to tidy with `rebase -i` first, then land the result with `--ff-only` so `main` stays linear and the merge is still recorded in the branch's history. Use `merge --squash` when you want a single commit on `main` and don't need the branch's history.
